title: Work and study
job: Explain what you do all day, and how
verifiedBy: LLM review, authorised by repo owner

rules.text: Arabic has no word for "of". Two nouns are pushed together and the second one owns the first: mudīr ash-sharika, "the manager of the company". That chain is the iḍāfa, and it is the shape behind almost every phrase in this module.

In a chain the FIRST noun never takes al-, the SECOND carries it, and the whole chain takes its definiteness from the second. bāb al-bayt is "the door of the house"; bāb bayt is "a door of a house"; al-bāb al-bayt is not Arabic at all. English puts "the" on both halves, and that is the habit to break.

The tāʾ marbūṭa is sounded in front of a second noun. shahāda alone ends on a plain -a; shahādat al-jāmiʿa sounds the t. It is the single most audible sign that a chain has been built rather than memorised.

yajibu an is impersonal: "it is necessary that I go", where English says "I must go". Nothing in it is you, and it never bends. yumkinu an is its twin for "it is possible", and both take L1-M3's an. The subjunctive mood beyond these two frames is L4's.

The plural comes with the word, not from a pattern. sharika gives sharikāt and muwaẓẓaf gives muwaẓẓafūn, but rātib gives rawātib — a shape nothing in rātib predicts. Each plural is listed on its own singular's row and learned there.

aʿmal and adrus are ordinary imperfect verbs on L1-M4's prefix law: a- for I, ta- for you or for she, ya- for he, na- for we. Only the roots are new here, and the person is still the front of the word.

sentences.cue: The manager of the company is busy today

words.note: Manager. As the first noun of a chain it never takes al-: mudīr ash-sharika. Standing alone and definite, it is al-mudīr.
Company. sh is a sun letter, so al- becomes ash-, exactly as in L1-M2's ash-shāy. The plural sharikāt is regular.

sentences.trap: English needs three words for this — the, of, the — and Arabic needs none of them. The relationship is the bare fact of the two nouns touching.
sentences.sound: mu-DEER ash-SHA-ri-ka — no pause between the two nouns; the chain is said as one word-group.

variations.cue: The door of the house is big
variations.changed: the same chain built from two words you have owned since L1: door and house

variations.cue: The head of the school is busy today
variations.changed: what is owned: ash-sharika → al-madrasa

mistake.why: English says "THE manager of THE company" and puts an article on each half. A chain allows only one, and it goes on the second noun: mudīr ash-sharika.

sentences.usage: The everyday way to name anyone by where they work, and the sentence to build the rest of the module on.
sentences.mnemonic: One article per chain, and it sits at the end.

sentences.cue: I work at a big company

words.note: "I work" — L2-M8's yaʿmal with L1-M4's a- prefix on the front, and L1-M4's ʿamal is the noun of it.

sentences.trap: English works "at" or "for" a company, and both tempt maʿa. Arabic works inside it: aʿmal fī sharika.
sentences.sound: AʿA-mal fee SHA-ri-ka — the ʿ closes the throat between the two a's, and it is what separates aʿmal from a plain amal.

variations.cue: I work at the company
variations.changed: a company becomes the company: only the article moved

variations.cue: We work at a big company
variations.changed: a- → na-: we, and nothing else in the sentence knows

mistake.why: maʿa is "with", and it is what English's "work for" reaches for. Arabic puts you inside the place: aʿmal fī sharika kabīra.

sentences.usage: The first thing anyone asks after your name, and the answer is four words long.
sentences.mnemonic: You are IN the company, not with it.

sentences.cue: I study Arabic at the university

words.note: "I study", on the prefix law you have had since L1-M4: a- for I, ta- for you or she, ya- for he. L1-M4's madrasa is the place of it.
The university — from a root meaning "to gather". English says "at university" with no article; Arabic keeps it: fī al-jāmiʿa.

sentences.trap: "At university" and "at school" go bare in English and never in Arabic. The article stays on, as it did for ilā al-madrasa in L1-M4.
sentences.sound: AD-rus al-JAA-mi-ʿa — the ʿ sits inside the word, just before the final -a, and it must be heard.

variations.cue: I study at the university
variations.changed: the subject dropped: only where the studying happens

variations.cue: He studies Arabic at the university
variations.changed: a- → ya-: he, and no pronoun anywhere

mistake.why: Bare jāmiʿa is "a university" — some university you have not named. Your own is al-jāmiʿa, with the article English drops.

sentences.usage: The student's half of the module, and it pairs with S02 as the two answers to "what do you do?"
sentences.mnemonic: al-jāmiʿa gathers people; darasa is what they do there.

sentences.cue: A university degree is very important

words.note: A certificate or degree. In front of a second noun the tāʾ marbūṭa sounds its t: shahādat al-jāmiʿa. Alone it ends on the plain -a.

sentences.trap: The -a you have written on every feminine noun since L1-M1 is not silent here. First in a chain, it becomes -at, and that t is the whole signal.
sentences.sound: sha-HAA-dat al-JAA-mi-ʿa — the t is pronounced and runs straight into the article.

variations.cue: A university degree is important
variations.changed: jiddan dropped: important, not very important

variations.cue: The certificate is very important
variations.changed: the chain undone: the noun alone takes its own article and its -a goes quiet again

mistake.why: Written the same way, said the wrong way. First in a chain, shahāda is shahādat — leaving the t off is what marks a phrase as memorised rather than built.

sentences.usage: Say it aloud twice: once as ash-shahāda and once as shahādat al-jāmiʿa. The t is the difference and it is audible.
sentences.mnemonic: A chain pulls the hidden t out of the -a.

sentences.cue: The employee at the company is always busy

words.note: An employee, bending the way every person-word does: muwaẓẓafa for a woman, muwaẓẓafūn for a group. The ẓ is the heavy dh, held at the back.

sentences.trap: A preposition is not a chain. al-muwaẓẓaf fī ash-sharika keeps both articles because fī stands between them; take fī away and the first article has to go.
sentences.sound: al-mu-WAẒ-ẓaf — the ẓ is doubled and heavy, the mouth wide and the tongue low.

variations.cue: The employee at the company is busy (a woman)
variations.changed: to a woman: muwaẓẓafa, and mashghūla follows it

variations.cue: The employees at the company are busy
variations.changed: one becomes many, and because they are people the adjective goes plural too

mistake.why: Two definite nouns side by side are neither a chain nor a sentence. Either drop the first article to build one — muwaẓẓaf ash-sharika, the company's employee — or put fī back between them.

sentences.usage: The line that tests whether the chain has landed: it looks like one and is not.
sentences.mnemonic: fī between them, articles on both; nothing between them, only one.

words.note: Salary. Its plural is rawātib — a shape nothing in rātib predicts, so it is learned here with the word and not built from it.

sentences.trap: English offers two shapes here — "the manager's salary" and "the salary of the manager" — and Arabic has only the chain. There is no 's and no min.
sentences.sound: RAA-tib al-mu-DEER — long ā at the front, and the chain runs on without a break.

variations.cue: The employee's salary is big
variations.changed: whose salary: al-mudīr → al-muwaẓẓaf

variations.cue: The salary is very big
variations.changed: the chain undone: rātib takes back its own article and owns nothing

mistake.why: min is "from" and "than", never "of". Nothing at all goes between the two nouns: rātib al-mudīr.

sentences.usage: Money talk in three words. It is also the shortest sentence in the module and the cleanest chain.
sentences.mnemonic: No word for "of" — just push them together.

sentences.cue: I have a meeting at four o'clock

words.note: A meeting — literally a gathering, from the same root as al-jāmiʿa. The plural ijtimāʿāt is regular.

sentences.trap: Arabic still has no verb "to have". ʿindī is L1-M7's "at me", and a meeting is something that sits at you rather than something you own.
sentences.sound: ij-ti-MAAʿ — the ʿ is the last sound of the word and must be heard, or it is a plain ijtimā.

variations.cue: I have a meeting with the manager of the company
variations.changed: the time becomes the person, and S01's chain comes back inside it

variations.cue: I have a meeting at the university tomorrow
variations.changed: when and where: four o'clock becomes tomorrow at the university

mistake.why: English drops "o'clock" and the hour stands alone. Arabic names the hour first — fī as-sāʿa ar-rābiʿa — or ar-rābiʿa is an ordinal describing nothing.

sentences.usage: The working day's most-repeated sentence, and it reuses L2-M6's clock without changing a thing.
sentences.mnemonic: ijtimāʿ and jāmiʿa both gather people.

sentences.cue: The exams at the university are hard

words.note: An exam, with the regular plural imtiḥānāt. The ḥ is the breathy h of L1-M2's bi-khayr, made in the throat.

sentences.trap: Exams are not people. A non-human plural takes a feminine singular adjective — ṣaʿba, not a plural one — which is L2-M3's law and does not relax at this length.
sentences.sound: al-im-ti-ḤAA-naat — the ḥ is a squeezed h, and the plural tail -āt is long.

variations.cue: The exam at the university is hard
variations.changed: many exams become one, and the adjective goes back to plain ṣaʿb

variations.cue: The Arabic exam is hard
variations.changed: a chain instead of a preposition: the exam OF Arabic

mistake.why: "Plural noun, plural adjective" is the English slogan, and it is wrong twice over: ṣaʿbūn is for people, and exams take the feminine singular ṣaʿba.

sentences.usage: The student's complaint, and the module's one reminder that L2-M3's agreement law is still running.
sentences.mnemonic: Things, however many, are treated as one she.

sentences.cue: I have to go to the meeting

words.note: "It is necessary", and there is no one in it. English's "I must" has an I; yajibu has no subject at all and never bends — the person lives in the verb after an.

sentences.trap: There is nothing here to translate "I" with. The obligation is stated impersonally and the person appears only in adhhab, at the far end of the sentence.
sentences.sound: YA-ji-bu an AD-hab — yajibu keeps its final -u, one of the few places this course writes one.

variations.cue: I have to study today
variations.changed: what is necessary: going becomes studying

variations.cue: You have to go to the meeting
variations.changed: who has to go: adhhab → tadhhab, and yajibu does not move at all

mistake.display: anā yajibu an adhhab ilā al-ijtimāʿ
mistake.script: أنا يجب أن أذهب إلى الاجتماع
mistake.why: The English "I must" pushes a pronoun to the front. yajibu is impersonal — it is necessary — and has no room for anā: yajibu an adhhab.

sentences.usage: The polite way to leave anywhere. Naming the necessity rather than yourself is what makes it sound like an obligation and not a whim.
sentences.mnemonic: It is necessary — not I am obliged.

words.note: "It is possible" — yajibu's twin, impersonal in the same way, and the bare stem behind L2-M1's yumkinuka. The an behind it is not optional.

sentences.trap: yajibu and yumkinu are one frame with two meanings, so anything you can say with must you can say with can — and neither ever takes a subject.
sentences.sound: YUM-ki-nu an AD-rus — the -nu tail is short, and an leans onto the verb behind it.

variations.cue: I can study at the university
variations.changed: where the studying can happen

variations.cue: I can't go today
variations.changed: negated: lā in front of yumkinu, and the rest of the frame holds

mistake.why: English's "can study" puts two verbs side by side and Arabic will not. an is the hinge L1-M3 taught after urīd, and yumkinu needs it too: yumkinu an adrus.

sentences.usage: The whole of this level's subjunctive: yajibu an and yumkinu an. Anything wider is L4's.
sentences.mnemonic: Same frame, two doors: must and can.

comprehensionPool.cue: The manager of the company is busy today
I work at a big company
I study Arabic at the university
A university degree is very important
The employee at the company is always busy
I have a meeting at four o'clock
The exams at the university are hard
I have to go to the meeting

comprehensionPool.display: mudīr ash-sharika yaʿmal fī al-jāmiʿa ayḍan
comprehensionPool.script: مدير الشركة يعمل في الجامعة أيضًا
comprehensionPool.cue: The manager of the company works at the university too

comprehensionPool.display: yajibu an adrus li-ʾanna al-imtiḥān ghadan
comprehensionPool.script: يجب أن أدرس لأن الامتحان غدًا
comprehensionPool.cue: I have to study because the exam is tomorrow
